Thanks for replying. I think the climate change debate has been poorly framed, and the right has foolishly attempted to to battle on a playing field that they can't win on. I want to toss my thoughts out there if you're open to looking at a different side of the issue.

We have some knowns. Atmospheric CO2 is increasing and the temperature has warmed by a fraction of a degree over the course of the century.

What is unknown or highly debated is how much this has effected weather patterns, how much it contributes toward more severe weather, how much of the temperature increase can be attributed to: solar variance, deeper cyclical weather patterns (like the one that brings ice ages at regular intervals), stationary weather recording locations (the urbanization that surrounds them increases temperature readings, and the movement of the magnetic poles, for example, last year the NP moved 57km toward Russia while weather stations moved 0km).

This all leads to the question that, if one accepts climate change (formerly global warming) is occurring, is it actually a bad thing? A hotter planet has more energy, in theory more energy in the atmosphere leads to more extreme weather, but it also leads to longer growing seasons, more available fresh water, better crop yields, and bigger denser forests.

It's worth noting that CO2 has an atmospheric lifetime of 5-30 years, while other gases like Nitrious Oxide and Methane are much more harmful because they linger in the air for far longer, up to 120 years, they have a considerably stronger warming effect, and are more dangerous to human health. While "particulate matter" is the pollution that affects human lung health, every climate agreement neglects to reign in "particulate matter" which is the actual danger to humans, and few even account for NOx and Me.

When Goldman Sachs thought up the carbon credit trading scheme as a way to make a new globally traded derivative, they aimed to get on the ground floor of an already corrupt system they had been the architects of. Then government gladly funds research that aims to support climate change, while little funding is applied toward the highly debated parts of climate change. So I hope you can at least see why people are skeptical. Especially as after they've been told in hyperbolic language, that "the maps of the world will need to be redrawn", or that San Francisco Bay will be underwater, or that "Global Warming is the equivalent of 400,000 Hiroshima Bombs a day."

I think the right could also approach this on free market and over regulation perspective, but they like a big powerful government just as much as the left so that's a long shot. I think everyone has the right to breathe clean air, that's why I'm frustrated that particulate matter is never addressed.
